text:
Engineering order drawing error: the section arrow points the wrong direction. Candidate labels are INCORRECT, MISMARKED, and REVERSED. The arrow is reversed in the drawing, so it is a documentation error. "INCORRECT" fits a documentation error best.

INCORRECT

The overwing exit overhead signs were installed backwards, so the passenger figure did not point outboard. That is an installation error. The label "REVERSED" also fits, but MISINSTALLED better captures the condition.

MISINSTALLED

Brake disc "coming apart" with one disc completely out points to disintegration rather than a simple break or crack.

DISINTEGRATED

The VEMD (Vehicle and Engine Multifunction Display) lane 2 display failed and could not be restored after shutdown and a power cycle. The unit was removed and replaced, so the part's condition is a display failure.

FAILED

Equipment cooling overheat indication at top of descent, with fault isolation finding no defects. The report centers on an overheat indication, which fits OVERHEATED better than INDICATION or WARNING LIGHT.

OVERHEATED

Battery pack found with low capacity → closest label is WEAK (battery weak), alternatives LOW or DEPLETED. "Low capacity" matches WEAK most directly.

WEAK

Engine rolled back at cruise, and the throttle had no authority. This points to a power loss on the left engine.

POWER LOSS

The row 13/14 emergency lights were inoperative because the batteries had drained. They were recharged, which indicates the battery was depleted.

DEPLETED

Disbonded → closest labels: DEBONDED, UNBONDED. "Disbonded" matches DEBONDED best.

DEBONDED

The report describes an existing repair found on the lower wing skin with no records. It was then repaired per the SRM (structural repair manual). The condition of the part is an undocumented prior repair, which fits DISCOVERED better than MISREPAIRED or DAMAGED.

DISCOVERED

The light was reported inoperative, and the fix was re-connecting its wire harness, which points to a disconnected harness as the defect. The candidate labels are DISCONNECTED and INOPERATIVE. The part's condition is best described by the cause, so DISCONNECTED fits better.

DISCONNECTED

Signs reported not illuminating, but the ops checks found all lights working, so the issue could not be reproduced. The fitting labels are "INOPERATIVE" or "NON ISSUE". The reported condition is that the part does not illuminate, so I'll go with INOPERATIVE.

INOPERATIVE

Of the labels describing this report, "MAKING METAL" fits best. The ECAM showed "oil chip detected" on engine 1, and the crew responded by replacing the scavenge filter and the electronic magnetic chip detector (EMCD). That points to metal particles in the oil, which is what "MAKING METAL" means. Other candidates like "WARNING MESSAGE" or "INDICATION" only describe how the problem was reported, not the condition itself.

MAKING METAL

Fault code reported... "torque motor signal out of range" — this is a fault message. Options: FAULT MESSAGE, OUT OF RANGE, FAULTED. The part was replaced; the condition reported is the fault. I'd choose FAULT MESSAGE.

FAULT MESSAGE

Excessive returns on one side only means the display is giving wrong information rather than being dead or showing a fault message, so the best fit is a false or inaccurate indication. Of FALSE INDICATION, INACCURATE, ERRATIC and MALFUNCTIONED, FALSE INDICATION fits best.

FALSE INDICATION

Both rear-seat master cylinders have a 3/16" deep, 1 1/2" long groove worn into the body. The groove comes from the cylinder contacting the rudder pedal mount whenever the pedal is actuated. The root cause is interference, but the failed part's condition is best described by the groove itself.

GROOVED

Liquid ingress in a composite elevator is usually found by NDT, and here it was repaired under an SRM Cat A procedure. Labels considered: CONTAMINATED, DAMAGED, DELAMINATED, DEBONDED. Liquid ingress in honeycomb is often tied to disbond, but nothing in the report states a disbond or delamination. The report describes moisture getting into the part, which fits CONTAMINATED best, though DAMAGED would also be defensible.

CONTAMINATED

Air was found in the water system and caused it not to pressurize, so the water was aerated.

AERATED

Mis-drilled holes are a manufacturing defect in the part itself, so this is a mismanufactured part.

MISMANUFACTURED

The oil inlet tube came disengaged from the heat exchanger because its retaining ring was not properly secured. The defect is the part coming apart from its connection, so the best fit is "DISENGAGED". "UNSECURE" was also a possibility, but the report explicitly says the tube "disengaged".

DISENGAGED

The best fit is WARNING MESSAGE. The crew received a "flaps fail" CAS message, and maintenance could not duplicate the problem, so no part was found in a defective state. The report centers on the message itself; FAULT MESSAGE was the other close candidate.

WARNING MESSAGE

Brake pressure only reached 1750 psi against a 2000 psi minimum, so the condition is low pressure at the brake unit.

LOW PRESSURE

The D ring on the L2 door was not visible and was corrected by repositioning it, so the part was out of place.

OUT OF POSITION

The failed part is the wire, which was found broken and then spliced. The light being inoperative is only the symptom, so the condition of the defective part is "broken."

BROKEN

The escape slide engagement light failed to illuminate, and foreign object debris (FOD) was found and removed from the proximity sensors and under the girt bar. Clearing the FOD restored normal operation, so FOD is the condition of the failed part.

FOD

Oxygen masks hanging down at row 32 means the mask panel opened and the masks deployed when they shouldn't have. The masks were stowed and no defects were found.

The deployment was unwanted, but the masks were found hanging rather than deploying in flight. That points to the panel being unlatched. Since the corrective action was stowing the masks and securing the panel, the closer fit is UNSECURE rather than UNWANTED DEPLOY.

The typical classification for "hanging" oxygen masks is likely UNWANTED DEPLOY or UNSECURE. "Panel secured" fits UNSECURE best.

UNSECURE

Loss of the RH electrical bus in flight, with power not restored by the APU. The best-fitting condition is power loss.

POWER LOSS

The part that failed is the cabin window, whose outer pane shattered in flight. The engine damage was a consequence of that failure. A shattered pane is best described as broken, though "failed" could also apply. Since the report says the window "failed in flight," FAILED is the closer match.

FAILED

Panel opened unexpectedly → oxygen mask deployment? The panel opened, not secured. Masks repacked. Candidates: UNWANTED DEPLOY, UNLATCHED, OPEN. The panel opened on its own, dropping the masks, which fits UNWANTED DEPLOY best.

UNWANTED DEPLOY

Flight crew corrected the bleed configuration and no maintenance was performed, so this points to crew error.

CREW ERROR

Runaway stab trim means the trim ran without being commanded, so it was uncontrollable. Relays R64 and R384 were replaced, and the DFCS BITE showed no faults. Of the available labels, UNCONTROLLABLE fits a runaway better than MALFUNCTIONED.

UNCONTROLLABLE

Missing arrow on sign — could be MISMANUFACTURED, INCORRECT, or WRONG PART. The defect is that the sign lacks the directional arrow, so the condition is likely INCORRECT (an incorrect sign was installed).

Alternatively, MISSING, but nothing fell off; the sign simply lacks the arrow. IMPROPER PART is another candidate. I'll go with INCORRECT.

INCORRECT

The report says no repair information was found for an existing repair to the doubler, so the repair had to be redone. That points to an improper or undocumented prior repair.

MISREPAIRED

Emergency lights did not illuminate because the batteries needed charging, so the failed condition is low battery charge. The closest label for that is DEPLETED.

DEPLETED

The oxygen panel door opened on landing without any mask dropping or oxygen being initiated. The fix was to resecure the door, so the failed condition is the door coming unlatched.

UNLATCHED

The lights failed their test because the wrong connectors had been installed, and the fault cleared once the correct connectors were fitted. That points to an improper part rather than a failed component. Between "WRONG PART" and "IMPROPER PART", "WRONG PART" matches the report's wording most directly.

WRONG PART

The IRU would not complete alignment after two attempts, so the core condition is a failure to align. The "dmp reversed" note refers to the deferral being cleared, not the part's condition. Of the candidate labels (INOPERATIVE, FAILED, MALFUNCTIONED), FAILED fits best.

FAILED

Clip not holding tight, fixed by adjustment, so OUT OF ADJUST fits best.

OUT OF ADJUST

Seats in row 10 reclined into the exit row, and the fix was adjusting the center bolt to restore the correct breakover force. That points to an adjustment problem.

OUT OF ADJUST

At FL340, engine #1 showed an EGT of 273° against 403° on engine #2, with all other indications normal. That points to an indication problem rather than a real temperature difference. The engine #1 EGT reads low.

READS LOW

Oil filter bypass alert led to in-flight shutdown. The part is the oil filter, with a bypass indication but no contamination found. "SHUTDOWN" fits the event best, with "BYPASSING" as the alternative. The filter bypass alert suggests the filter was bypassing, but these reports typically classify in-flight engine shutdowns as SHUTDOWN.

SHUTDOWN

Pulled strands on a composite floor panel skin describe fibers pulled out of the surface. Candidates are "PULLED", "FRAYED" and "DAMAGED"; "PULLED" matches the report's wording most directly.

PULLED

The failed part is the No. 1 pack valve, which was found opening and closing intermittently without being commanded. The overtemp messages were symptoms of that valve fault, so the condition is intermittent.

INTERMITTENT

The condition of the part is best described as FAILED, since the report states the reduction gearbox had an internal failure.

FAILED

The report says the APU fire bottle "discharged" light came on after takeoff. That points to the bottle condition being discharged, though it could also be read as an indication-type event (ILLUMINATED or FALSE INDICATION). The part condition reported is the discharged bottle, so DISCHARGED fits best.

DISCHARGED

"Date off" means the bottle's date had lapsed, so the condition is OUT OF DATE rather than EXPIRED.

OUT OF DATE

Slide deployed inside the aft galley, which points to an inadvertent deployment rather than an intended one.

UNWANTED DEPLOY

Holes with short edge margin and a hole riding on the fitting radius point to a manufacturing or installation defect. Since this was found during a shear tie install mod, MISMANUFACTURED or MECHANIC ERROR are the candidates. In SDR data, short edge margin findings are typically classified as out of limits, so OUT OF LIMITS fits best.

OUT OF LIMITS

Door assist bottles needed nitrogen servicing, meaning their pressure was low.

LOW PRESSURE

Existing doubler repair was evaluated and found not conforming to the SRM, so the prior repair was improperly done.

MISREPAIRED

"Not attached to structure" could map to DETACHED or UNSECURE; DETACHED is the more direct fit.

DETACHED

The crew's report describes the landing gear symptoms, but the label should reflect the condition of the part found defective. Maintenance traced the fault to low servicing of the nose landing gear (NLG) strut. Between LOW and UNDERSERVICED, UNDERSERVICED fits better because the finding is that the strut had not been serviced to the required level.

UNDERSERVICED

Lav F fire bottle reads 0 psi, so the bottle has been discharged or depleted. Candidate labels are DISCHARGED, DEPLETED, LOW PRESSURE and READS LOW. A reading of 0 psi most often means the bottle has discharged. "Reads low" would suggest a gauge error, which doesn't fit here. DISCHARGED is the best match.

DISCHARGED

The condition of the part that failed is the connector, which was found disengaged and reconnected.

DISENGAGED

Light hanging out, then secured — the part's condition was not properly fastened.

UNSECURE

Slide came out of its container and had to be repacked. UNPACKED is a possible fit, but DISPLACED matches the wording "displaced from container" directly.

DISPLACED

The maintenance message says the RVDT signal "is out of range," so the label is taken directly from that wording.

OUT OF RANGE

Emergency lights stayed on because the G switches (impact-activated switches) had been triggered, and resetting them turned the lights off. The part's condition is therefore best described as activated.

ACTIVATED

The failed part is the 100 amp hydraulic pump circuit breaker, which maintenance found open. The two closest labels are "TRIPPED" and "OPEN". "TRIPPED" fits a circuit breaker that has popped, but "OPEN" matches the report's own wording.

OPEN

Oxygen mask door opened and masks were repacked; the condition is masks deployed/door opened. Of the options DEPLOYED, UNWANTED DEPLOY and UNPACKED, UNWANTED DEPLOY fits a door that dropped open uncommanded.

UNWANTED DEPLOY

The failed part is the APU. About two minutes after it started, it shut down and the low oil pressure light came on. Maintenance then serviced the APU oil, so low oil was the likely cause. However, the reported condition is the APU shutting itself down, which fits AUTO SHUTDOWN better than LOW QUANTITY.

AUTO SHUTDOWN

The report describes a failed autoland on an approach with calm wind and a clear ILS critical area, which points to the system itself rather than outside interference. Troubleshooting found no fault, but the autoland did not work. The best fit for that condition is "failed."

FAILED

Label for the failed part's condition: the Korry switch bracket made contact and burnt up the contact point, and the report is coded "smke" with smoke emitted. The candidate labels are SMOKE, BURNED and SHORTED. The report code "smke" points to SMOKE as the primary condition.

SMOKE

Door difficult to open and close points to a binding condition; the guide arm and locking cam were replaced.

BINDS

Door assist bottle needed servicing, meaning its pressure was low. LOW PRESSURE fits best.

LOW PRESSURE

Bulb out → typically "INOPERATIVE" or "BURNED OUT". A bulb that is out is best described as burned out.

BURNED OUT

Gear failed to retract on selection, and a master warning appeared. The key condition is the warning message, but the gear itself didn't respond. "LG LEVER DISAG" is a disagreement warning message, so that label fits best.

WARNING MESSAGE

Squeal from the door, then loss of cabin pressure; the inflatable door seal was replaced. That points to the seal leaking.

LEAKING

Electrical fire suspected; wiring damaged and determined to have caused the damage. The failed part is the in-seat power wiring, and its condition is "damaged." An alternative is BURNED, but the report explicitly says "wiring... damaged," so DAMAGED is the closer fit.

DAMAGED

The exit signs were the wrong type, missing the direction arrows. That points to INCORRECT or IMPROPER PART. The report itself says "incorrect," so INCORRECT fits best.

INCORRECT

Panel departed the aircraft in flight → INFLT SEPARATION.

INFLT SEPARATION

Loud sound, torque loss and an ITT rise led the crew to shut the left engine down as a precaution. The failed part's condition isn't identified yet; the defining event is the precautionary shutdown. Options are SHUTDOWN, PRECAUTIONARY or POWER LOSS, and the shutdown is the best fit for what is reported.

SHUTDOWN

The report says the precooler was found "damaged and leaking," which allows two labels. The cabin odor is the symptom, and leaking is the condition that caused it, so LEAKING is the better fit.

LEAKING

Rejected takeoff with hot brakes, but the inspections found tires and brakes undamaged and the AFS tests passed, so no part was defective. This fits HOT or PRECAUTIONARY; HOT best matches the reported brake condition.

HOT

Magnetic particle inspection is a crack-detection method, so a "surface indication" found this way most likely means a crack. Other labels were considered: INDICATION is literal but refers to cockpit indications, and FAILED INSP could fit.

CRACKED

Of the available labels, MISALIGNED fits best: the end cap did not match up with the newly installed skin, which points to a fit or alignment mismatch. IMPROPER PART or WRONG PART could also apply, but the report doesn't say the part was wrong.

MISALIGNED

Gauge in red band means bottle pressure low.

LOW PRESSURE

Light was inoperative; the fix was cleaning debris and buildup from the girt bar track and prox switches. That cause points to contamination, but the report frames the failure as the arm light being inop, so the reported condition is the light not working.

INOPERATIVE

This report is about an aft halon fire extinguisher that was used (discharged), and the corrective action was to remove and replace it. The list includes both USED and DISCHARGED. USED matches the report's own wording most directly, so I chose it.

USED

The report says the slide light stayed on even though the door was disarmed, so the light was giving a false reading. Recycling the arming handle cleared it.

FALSE INDICATION

Passengers reported a smell of smoke, so this is an odor report rather than visible smoke.

ODOR

The slide was reported as dislodged, but further inspection found it serviceable and it was simply re-installed, so no actual defect existed.

NON ISSUE

Ground crew failed to install the tail stand and the aircraft tipped onto its tail. That is a handler error.

HANDLER ERROR

Switch found left in ON position, which depleted the emergency light battery. The failed part's condition is best described as out of position.

OUT OF POSITION

Cam pins failed a dimension check, which points to wear, but the report never says "worn." It only says they failed the check, so either FAILED INSP or OUT OF LIMITS could apply. Since the report frames the finding as a failed dimension check during inspection, FAILED INSP fits best.

FAILED INSP

The report centers on a maintenance message stating the bleed FAMV RVDT left signal is "out of range," which matches the OUT OF RANGE label directly.

OUT OF RANGE

The report describes a brake overheat EICAS message that appeared multiple times. Troubleshooting attributed it to extreme brake use, and no maintenance action was required. The condition that best fits is the brake overheating itself, rather than a defect requiring repair.

OVERHEATED

The failed part is the pressure switch. The low pressure light came on intermittently even though the pump was verified running, which points to an intermittent switch rather than a pump fault.

INTERMITTENT

Lavatory door difficult to open/close, fixed by lubing. "STIFF" or "BINDS" or "LACK OF LUBE". Difficult to operate suggests BINDS or STIFF. The remedy was lube, so LACK OF LUBE is possible, but the condition reported is difficulty operating. I'd pick BINDS.

BINDS

Sign lacks a direction arrow, so a feature of the part is absent. MISSING fits best, though MISMANUFACTURED is possible.

MISSING

Several CAS messages posted at once (pitch trim, yaw damp, mach trim), and ground checks could not duplicate the problem. The condition is best described by the multiple indications.

MULTIPLE IND

Binding and ratcheting are both described; the primary condition is binding.

BINDS

EGT exceeded limits on takeoff → OVERTEMP. Probes and harness were replaced, which could suggest a FALSE INDICATION, but the report doesn't state the probes were defective. The reported condition is the overtemp.

OVERTEMP

Door will not close — likely binding/stuck? Fairing access door replaced. Probably DAMAGED, but not stated. "Will not close" could be INOPERATIVE or BINDS. Common SDR label for that wording is FAILED or INOPERATIVE. I'd pick INOPERATIVE.

INOPERATIVE

Door 1L did not show armed because lining panel 831CZ had been installed incorrectly; re-installing it correctly fixed the indication. The failed part is the panel, and its condition is an incorrect installation.

MISINSTALLED

Grit from the runway coated the brakes, which points to "CONTAMINATED." "DIRTY" was also possible, but "CONTAMINATED" describes this condition more precisely.

CONTAMINATED

Multiple simultaneous EICAS messages across several systems point to a multiple-failure event rather than a single failed part.

MULTIPLE FAIL

Classifying the cable's condition: the elevator control cable is rubbing against the pulley bracket. That rubbing wear is chafing, so CHAFED fits best. The cause given (bad installation) could suggest MISINSTALLED, but the condition actually found on the part is the rubbing.

CHAFED

Safety pin could not be aligned on the slide, which points to a misalignment condition.

MISALIGNED

The defect being reported is the replacement torque tube, not the original crack. The new part arrived from the manufacturer improperly assembled, with 14 of 18 rivets below minimum dimension, and Textron pulled all of that part number from stock for the same issue. That makes it a manufacturing defect.

MISMANUFACTURED

Mask needed resetting and was repacked, which suggests it had come unpacked or deployed. "UNPACKED" fits best, since the corrective action was repacking.

UNPACKED

Cover was in the incorrect position, so the best label is misinstalled. Other options considered: "OUT OF POSITION" or "INCORRECT". The report says "found to be in the incorrect ... position", and the fix was to install per the AMM. That points to MISINSTALLED.

MISINSTALLED

Of the available labels, LEAKING best fits a window that failed to seal and let air through the seam. The high-pitch sound is a symptom of that air leak.

LEAKING

The report describes an odor in the passenger cabin, but the defective part is the APU gearbox magnetic plug drain O-ring, which was leaking oil. Classifying by the condition of the failed part points to the leak rather than the odor.

LEAKING

Of the two door micro switches tested, 13WN was found sticky with anti-corrosion compound and had to be cleaned. That points to the switch being contaminated by foreign material rather than electrically or mechanically failed; both switches otherwise checked good. Alternatives were STICKING, which describes the symptom rather than the condition, and FALSE INDICATION, which describes the light rather than the part. CONTAMINATED best captures the part's condition.

CONTAMINATED

Labels include DEBONDED and UNBONDED; "disbonded" maps to DEBONDED.

DEBONDED

The engine lost power on its own: N1 spun down to 15–17% with no fire or seizure, and it was later restarted. That is an uncommanded in-flight flameout or rollback. The crew securing the engine happened only after the fact, so "SHUTDOWN" fits less well, and "POWER LOSS" is a broader alternative. The best match for a spontaneous spool-down with a successful relight is "FLAMED OUT".

FLAMED OUT

Failed operational test of damping function — "FAILED" or "FAILED INSP"? An operational test failure is closest to FAILED.

FAILED

Suspected leak was really a fuel quantity imbalance indication; the fix was replacing the fuel quantity processor. The part (processor) gave a wrong or imbalanced reading, which fits FALSE INDICATION better than INACCURATE.

FALSE INDICATION

Door assist cylinder pressure reads zero, so the reservoir lost pressure. LOW PRESSURE or PRESSURE LOSS both fit; a zero reading on the reservoir is best described as PRESSURE LOSS.

PRESSURE LOSS

The report says the PA is very quiet from the 1R interphone, which is a weak output rather than a total failure. "WEAK" fits a low-volume condition best.

WEAK

Nose wheel was 30 degrees left after takeoff instead of centered, so it was not in its correct position. Candidates are MISALIGNED, OUT OF POSITION, or OUT OF RIG; OUT OF POSITION best describes a wheel not centered.

OUT OF POSITION

Applying the label definitions to this report:

- The door would not fall freely and had to be pushed 2-3 inches before it free fell.
- The fix was cleaning the door seal mating surfaces, which points to the seal adhering to its mating surface.
- That condition is "STICKING" (or "STICKS"). "BINDS" is also possible, but sticking describes a seal holding the door better.

STICKING

Panel departed the aircraft in flight, which matches the in-flight separation label.

INFLT SEPARATION

Sparks are listed first and are the most specific condition reported for the glareshield panel; smoke is secondary.

SPARKS

The part that failed is the fan shaft seal, and the evidence is oil wetting under the left engine spinner, which points to a leaking seal. The odor is the symptom; the condition of the defective part is the leak.

LEAKING

The light strips have discolored areas that fail to illuminate. The non-illumination is the functional defect, but the report leads with discoloration as the observed condition of the part. Choosing between DISCOLORED and INOPERATIVE, the observed physical condition is the discoloration, so that label fits best.

DISCOLORED

Part condition: the light was found dangling (unsecured) and inoperative. Dangling suggests a mounting problem, which could fit DETACHED, LOOSE or UNSECURE. "Inoperative" is also given, and these reports are often classified as INOPERATIVE. Since the light is listed first as dangling, I'll go with the mounting condition, LOOSE.

LOOSE

Unusual noise and higher-than-normal resistance were cleared by lubricating the hinges, so the root cause was insufficient lubrication.

LACK OF LUBE

Most likely, the left main uplock box failed to lock the gear. Candidate labels are UNLOCKED, ILLUMINATED, FAILED and MALFUNCTIONED. The report describes an unlock light showing on two panels, and the part was replaced. The light came on because the gear did not lock, so the part's condition is best described as UNLOCKED.

UNLOCKED

Wavy floor panel → DEFORMED or WARPED. "Wavy" suggests a panel that is no longer flat, and DEFORMED is the broader, more common label for this kind of condition.

DEFORMED

Security lacing and pin undone — "UNLACED" fits.

UNLACED

Slide deployed but did not inflate properly or fully, even with manual inflation → partial deploy.

PARTIAL DEPLOY

The control plate on the forward passenger door's pneumatic assembly was found installed in the disarmed position while the aircraft was in service. That means the part was put in wrong, so MISINSTALLED fits best. DEACTIVATED was also considered, but the root cause here is the incorrect installation.

MISINSTALLED

The cockpit trim air valve was "showing xx," which means a dashed or invalid display and points to a fault indication. The closest label could be FAULTY, FAULT MESSAGE or INOPERATIVE. An "xx" display on the ECAM is commonly classified as FAILED or FAULTED. The report gives only the indication, with no actual failure described, so INDICATION is the best fit.

INDICATION

The defect is the L1 door intermittently showing unarmed during flight, and pushing the arm lever restored the indication. That points to an intermittent fault rather than a part that will not arm at all.

INTERMITTENT

Exit sign lenses had arrows and were replaced with the proper no-arrow lens, so the wrong part was installed.

Options: IMPROPER PART, WRONG PART. Both fit; WRONG PART is the more common choice for an incorrect part installed.

WRONG PART

Main gearbox bypass light illuminated; the reported condition is the light illuminating.

ILLUMINATED

The report describes a fuel imbalance indication with the left tank reading 1,200 lbs low. This could be a true imbalance, a leak, or a false indication, and the root cause is still open. The condition reported is the indication itself, so the best fit is INDICATION.

INDICATION

Disbond of the skin maps most closely to "DEBONDED" (the alternative, "UNBONDED", fits less well).

DEBONDED

The report gives two findings for the P4.95 tube: it was found loose, and it was damaged. Looseness is the specific defect that caused the lost EPR indication, so it is the better label than the more general damage.

LOOSE

Sheet metal on the left engine inboard core cowl is described as "tearing off," with "ripped metal," so the best match is TORN.

TORN

Unsafe indication, flickering light, actuator replaced. The failed part is the actuator, and its failure condition is not stated, so the label should reflect the reported symptom. "INDICATION" fits the unsafe indication best; "INTERMITTENT" is the alternative suggested by the flickering light, but the core report is the unsafe indication.

INDICATION

The report describes a fuel imbalance of more than 1200 lbs noticed during climb. The cause and the failed part are not yet identified. The closest condition is fuel being out of balance between tanks.

OUT OF BALANCE

Part of the forward entry door slide sticks out from under the slide when the door is armed. The fix was adjusting the girt bar, which points to the slide being out of position or improperly stowed. "IMPROPER STOW" is the closest fit for a slide that is not stowed correctly.

IMPROPER STOW

The failed part is the wire at seat connector D9724J, which was found shorted. The emergency light being inoperative was only the symptom of that short.

SHORTED

Cover will not stay attached, so the fit is not holding. Candidate labels are UNSECURE, LOOSE and DETACHED. It was reinstalled and resecured, which points to UNSECURE.

UNSECURE

Red lights flashing at the doors with the engines off and the cabin depressurized point to a false cabin pressure warning, and the lights later stopped flashing. That makes this an erroneous indication. The closest options are FALSE INDICATION, WARNING LIGHT and INTERMITTENT, and FALSE INDICATION fits best.

FALSE INDICATION

Window arced then cracked. The failed part condition: cracked is the outcome for the window, which was replaced.

CRACKED

Connector not fully engaged — options: NOT SEATED, DISENGAGED, LOOSE, UNSECURE. The fix was to "resecure" it, but "not fully engaged" maps most directly to NOT SEATED.

NOT SEATED

Part is the throttle cable, found totally broken with no wear; "fatigue break" suggests FATIGUED, but the report's main observed condition is the break itself.

BROKEN

The report describes a hot brakes caution with high temperatures on the left truck, but the functional test then passed. That makes it hard to say whether the brakes were truly overheated or the indication was false. The core reported condition is high brake temperature, so the label is "HOT".

HOT

Bottle required servicing — low pressure? Underserviced? The door assist bottle needed servicing to full, implying low pressure/quantity. "LOW PRESSURE" fits a gas bottle.

LOW PRESSURE

The report describes a smell ("dirty sock smell") and the troubleshooting found no defects. ODOR fits that better than FUMES.

ODOR

This report describes a documentation error in an engineering order (EO). The section cut arrow points the wrong direction, and the gap was given as 0.60 instead of 0.060. The defective item is the document itself, so the best fit is INCORRECT.

INCORRECT

The part being classified is the RH engine #1 igniter plug, which was found "bad" and replaced. A slip joint pneumatic leak was also noted, but that was referred to a separate log page and is not the part in question here. "Bad" gives no specific failure mode, so the closest general label is "FAULTY" rather than "FAILED".

FAULTY

The door was hard to open, which points to the part being either stiff or binding. Maintenance fixed it by adjusting the door per the AMM, so the condition is best captured as out of adjustment.

OUT OF ADJUST

Brakes ran hot (980C) and felt as if rubbing, and the fix was replacing the alternate brake manifold. "Rubbing" points to DRAGGING, but the reported condition is the high temperature, so HOT fits best.

HOT

Both the haze and the musty smell are mentioned. The haze cleared and only the odor recurred on descent, so the odor is the persistent, primary condition.

ODOR

Installed backwards means the part was installed incorrectly.

MISINSTALLED

The oxygen masks dropped without being commanded, so the condition is an unwanted deployment.

UNWANTED DEPLOY

Diverted for oil quantity loss; no leaks found; borescope showed coking and debris in the 5/6 bearing compartment. The oil was being consumed internally, which fits OIL CONSUMPTION.

OIL CONSUMPTION

Oil quantity went to zero and the crew shut down the engine precautionarily. Candidate labels include LOW QUANTITY, SHUTDOWN, PRECAUTIONARY, PRESSURE LOSS and LEAKING. The failed part is the engine, which suffered oil loss, and the event was a precautionary shutdown. Shutdown reports like this are typically coded as SHUTDOWN.

SHUTDOWN

The part that failed is the T49.5 probe, and the report says its resistance was "out of limits." The high EGT reading came from that probe, but the condition actually found on the part was the out-of-limits resistance.

OUT OF LIMITS

The failed part's condition is that the APU oil system was found overserviced, which caused the oil leak and the odor. The odor is only the symptom, so the part condition is overserviced.

OVERSERVICED

The report centres on a smoke and burning-odor event in the cabin, also noticed in the cockpit. Troubleshooting found no leaks and no smell, so there is no confirmed defective part. The reported condition is smoke, which is the primary symptom described.

SMOKE

Mt204 is a bleed duct temperature sensor, and the report says it was found touching the airframe, so its position was adjusted to fix it. Labels like INTERFERENCE, OUT OF POSITION and WARNING LIGHT all fit to some degree. Since the part's condition was being in the wrong place, OUT OF POSITION fits best.

OUT OF POSITION

Several labels fit parts of this report:

- **WARNING MESSAGE**: the "rev disagree" message triggered the abort.
- **SURGES**: the ops check found the valve surging.
- **LEAKING**: a small leak was found on the #100 ICU (isolation control unit).

The task is to label the condition of the part found defective. The ICU was replaced because of the leak and the surging valve. Of these, the surging valve is the malfunction that best explains the disagree message, so it is the most likely root cause.

SURGES

Debris was found obstructing the grit bar sensor, which kept the slide light from illuminating. The part's condition is therefore best described as obstructed.

OBSTRUCTED

The emergency exit light stayed on even though the switch was in the arm position. That points to a failed switch, which was replaced. The best fit for the switch's condition is generic.

FAILED

Flaps would not retract after landing, giving a split-flap condition, and the #5 tee angle gearbox was replaced. "SPLIT" here names the flap asymmetry rather than the condition of the failed part. The gearbox is the defective part, but the report gives no specific failure mode for it, so the general label fits best.

FAILED

Floor panel "disbonded" maps most directly to DEBONDED.

DEBONDED

The report says wire 2751-4528 was found damaged between the right wing tip brake and 4008, and it was fixed with a grade 1a wire repair. The flaps locking is the symptom. The defective part is the wire, and its condition is described as "damage" (the word "broke" refers to the wing tip brake). The best label is therefore DAMAGED rather than the other options considered: LOCKED, OPEN or BROKEN.

DAMAGED

The tow bar broke during push back, so the failed part's condition is broken.

BROKEN

Label: MALFUNCTIONED

The FMS behaved wrongly rather than failing outright: it loaded only the back course and activated a localizer when LNAV was pressed. Troubleshooting found no faults and the problem could not be duplicated. "OUT OF SEQUENCE" was considered but describes timing rather than this kind of wrong behavior, and "ERRATIC" does not fit because the error repeated the same way every time.

MALFUNCTIONED

The part that failed is the gearbox vent line fitting, and the report says it was blocked. The fumes and the oil around the APU were consequences of that blockage, so the label describes the fitting's condition rather than the symptoms.

BLOCKED

The part that failed is the D03114P connector. Pin 11 was found short-circuited and the connector was replaced. The dim light was only the symptom, so the label for the failed part's condition is SHORTED.

SHORTED

Low oil pressure is the primary condition reported; the warning and the engine shutdown both followed from it.

LOW PRESSURE

Mask deployed without command during takeoff — UNWANTED DEPLOY fits better than DEPLOYED.

UNWANTED DEPLOY

Fuel gauges showed 1/4 remaining while the tanks were actually near empty, so the failed part is the gauge giving inaccurate readings. That points to "READS HIGH" or "INACCURATE". The gauges overstated the fuel quantity, so READS HIGH is the more specific fit.

READS HIGH

Most likely MISOVERHAULED, since the encoding altimeter was just received after overhaul and failed its functional check. It sent incorrect altitude information to the transponder. A defect found on receipt after overhaul points to the overhaul itself.

MISOVERHAULED

Oxygen mask compartment opened on its own, which corresponds to unwanted deployment of the masks.

The candidate labels are "OPEN", "UNWANTED DEPLOY" and "DEPLOYED". "UNWANTED DEPLOY" best describes a compartment that opened when it shouldn't have.

UNWANTED DEPLOY

Liner had come loose and blocked the view of the indication flag; the fix was resecuring it, so the failed condition is the liner being unsecure rather than the flag itself.

UNSECURE

Fuel quantity indication error: the left side read low compared with the right, then returned to normal later in the flight, and BITE checks found no fault. That points to a false or erroneous indication. Candidates are FALSE INDICATION, READS LOW and INTERMITTENT. The ECAM alerted a fuel indication error, and the left-side reading was about 4000 lbs lower than the right, so READS LOW is the closest fit.

READS LOW

Rigging adjustment fixed the door, so the condition is OUT OF RIG or OUT OF ADJUST. OUT OF RIG fits rigging best.

OUT OF RIG

This is a documentation error in an engineering order: the section arrow points the wrong way and the gap value is wrong (0.60 instead of 0.060). The fitting label is INCORRECT.

INCORRECT

The report says the door bottle pressure read 0 psi and was fixed by servicing it back to operating pressure. That points to pressure loss rather than a part being missing or the bottle being merely empty. Candidate labels were LOW PRESSURE, PRESSURE LOSS, DEPLETED and EMPTY. At 0 psi the bottle has lost its pressure entirely, so PRESSURE LOSS fits best.

PRESSURE LOSS

Peeled upper surface layer fibers on a composite floor panel could be read as delamination, but the report describes the surface layer as peeling, so the closest label is "PEELING".

PEELING

The failed part is the exhaust system downstream of the muffler. A crack there had been fixed with an unapproved weld, and that faulty weld repair led to the burned hole. Since the root defect is the improper repair rather than the crack itself, the best label is MISREPAIRED.

MISREPAIRED

The reservoir discharged unexpectedly while maintenance was installing the safety pin, so the key event is an inadvertent slide deployment. The slide only went out half way, which makes PARTIAL DEPLOY a possible label, but the failure itself is the unintended deployment.

UNWANTED DEPLOY

Slide partially deployed during catering door closure — "PARTIAL DEPLOY" fits best (vs. UNWANTED DEPLOY). The deployment was unwanted, but the most specific condition described is a partial deployment.

PARTIAL DEPLOY

Gust lock will not engage — closest label: "FAILED"? Options: INOPERATIVE, MALFUNCTIONED, DISENGAGED. "Will not engage" maps commonly to INOPERATIVE or MALFUNCTIONED. I'd choose MALFUNCTIONED.

MALFUNCTIONED

The part that failed is the overhead bin latch at row 10. The bin door was inoperative and had to be taped closed. That points to INOPERATIVE.

INOPERATIVE

The crew shut the engine down in flight after an oil filter bypass indication. On inspection there was no debris, and the filter pop-out indicator did not show a bypass, so the indication may have been false. Even so, the reported event is the oil filter bypass, and the scavenge filter was replaced. That makes the part condition the bypass itself rather than the shutdown or a false indication.

BYPASSING

Window would not open; fixed by cleaning and lubrication, which suggests it was sticking. Candidates are NOT OPENED, STUCK, and LACK OF LUBE. Since the report describes the window failing to open, STUCK fits best.

STUCK

The failed condition is the axle nuts on the #1 and #2 nose gear tires, which were not torqued to specification. That points to under-torque rather than the vibration symptom itself.

UNDERTORQUED

Floor panel upper surface layer fibers peeled — this most closely matches PEELING, though DELAMINATED would also be plausible.

PEELING

The #3 main brake assembly was found seized, and the aircraft could not move under power. The list has no "SEIZED" label. The closest matches are LOCKED, FROZEN, STUCK and JAMMED. A seized brake that won't release fits STUCK or LOCKED. I chose LOCKED, since a brake that is locked up and won't turn describes this condition best.

LOCKED

The report centres on an ECAM message, "AIR ENG 2 BLEED HI TEMP", and the condition behind it is a bleed over-temperature. OVERTEMP fits that best; WARNING MESSAGE is the alternative, but it describes the alert rather than the part's condition.

OVERTEMP

Of the candidate labels, "LEAKING" is ruled out because the report says the leak was recent and does not confirm a current one. "UNBALANCED" fits better, since the condition actually reported is a fuel imbalance between the left and right tanks.

UNBALANCED

The report describes the electric stab trim running nose up on its own, with no pilot command, until the clacker sounded. That is a runaway trim, an uncommanded movement. Of the available labels, MALFUNCTIONED fits this condition best; UNCONTROLLABLE was also considered.

MALFUNCTIONED

The squat switch gave the wrong indication: it showed on ground while the aircraft was in the air. It produced a WOW miscompare that came and went. It ohmed out good on the ground but was replaced anyway. The candidate labels are INTERMITTENT, FALSE INDICATION and FAULTY. The behavior was intermittent: the first jack-up showed the wrong state, and the second showed it correctly. The narrative calls the part "damaged," but the core issue is a false on-ground indication that recurred only some of the time.

INTERMITTENT

Light not locked into receptacle → NOT SEATED.

NOT SEATED

Difficult to arm suggests binding or stiffness rather than a complete failure to arm. The fix was cleaning and lubricating the floor mounts, which points to lack of lube or stiffness. "Difficult" fits STIFF better than WILL NOT ARM.

STIFF

Missed drill hole means a hole drilled in the wrong place, which is a manufacturing defect.

MISMANUFACTURED

Autothrottle disconnected during takeoff; fix was replacing the left FMC. The condition could be DISENGAGED or FAILED. The report states the autothrottle disconnect as an event, which is the observed condition.

DISENGAGED

The finding was that the APU plenum was contaminated, which caused the smell.

CONTAMINATED

The report says the gap between the inner chord and stringer S-18A measured 0.029 inch. That exceeds the 0.006 inch limit, and the corrective action was shimming the gap. A measurement beyond an allowed limit fits OUT OF TOLERANCE or OUT OF LIMITS; I chose OUT OF LIMITS.

OUT OF LIMITS

Key facts in the report:
- A gear disagree warning repeated four times and then cleared, which describes an intermittent fault.
- The troubleshooting identified the PSEU as possibly unserviceable, and it was replaced.

The failed part is the PSEU. Candidate labels are FALSE INDICATION, UNSERVICEABLE, INTERMITTENT and WARNING LIGHT. The report itself calls the PSEU "unserviceable" and describes a false gear disagree warning. Because the PSEU is the part being classified, UNSERVICEABLE fits best.

UNSERVICEABLE

Slide fell out of pack — the slide came out of its packed state. Best fits UNPACKED.

UNPACKED

Low capacity battery pack → options: LOW, WEAK, DEPLETED. A battery pack with low capacity is best described as WEAK.

WEAK

Generator amperage reading lower than the other generator; the transformer was replaced. The part's condition is best described as "READS LOW"? Or "OUT OF TOLERANCE"? An amp split is a load-sharing imbalance, but "READS LOW" fits best.

READS LOW

Of the conditions reported, "Not fully latched" (rollers not engaged) is the clearest candidate, but the root cause was that the door was not parallel. The fix was a guide arm adjustment, which points to OUT OF ADJUST. UNLATCHED is a possible alternative. Since the corrective action was an adjustment, OUT OF ADJUST fits best.

OUT OF ADJUST

Bulging and cracked fastener holes — cracked is the primary structural condition.

CRACKED

Girt bar rubbing during door closing is contact between parts, best fit is INTERFERENCE (CHAFED is an alternative but implies wear damage, which isn't stated).

INTERFERENCE

The report says the life vest seal "opened and ruptured," which points to RUPTURED as the condition of the failed part.

RUPTURED

Slide falling out of container; small flap repositioned. Could be "UNPACKED", "DISPLACED", or "OUT OF POSITION". The slide was coming out of its pack, so "UNPACKED" fits best.

UNPACKED

Of the conditions in the report (exposed, broken, severed), the wire found at row 14 was severed, which is what caused the emergency light failure.

SEVERED

Fuel moving from the right outer tank into both inner tanks points to a valve that is passing fuel when it should be closed. That is an internal leak through the valve, so the best fit is BYPASSING.

BYPASSING

Typical SDR wording for shear ties is "cracked," but this report names the part and location without stating a defect, so CRACKED is an assumption based on the most common shear tie finding.

CRACKED

Flaps locked out; the part replaced was the RH flap position transmitter. The report says nothing about how the transmitter failed, so the condition is best taken from the reported symptom, the flaps locking out.

LOCKED

Window will not lock, and lubrication was the fix, which points to lack of lube; but the condition reported is the window failing to lock. Of the available labels, "UNLOCKED" matches that best.

UNLOCKED

Indication temporarily went to zero and then self-cleared after a few minutes, so the fault was transient and could not be duplicated on the ground. That points to an intermittent condition.

INTERMITTENT

Overspeed caution light came on during run-up, but the fix was replacing the tachometer box. That points to a false or spurious indication rather than a real overspeed. The candidates are "FALSE INDICATION", "WARNING LIGHT", "ILLUMINATED" and "OVERSPEED". The report describes the light illuminating with no stated cause beyond it, so "ILLUMINATED" fits most directly, though "FALSE INDICATION" is also plausible.

ILLUMINATED

Emergency light batteries found drained, then recharged and checked good. The best-fitting label for a drained battery is DEPLETED.

DEPLETED

Switch "hard to toggle" describes a part that is stiff, so STIFF fits better than BINDS or STICKING.

STIFF

Door difficult to open; fixed by adjusting the control rod, so the part was out of adjustment.

OUT OF ADJUST

The report says the upper pylon blowout panel was found open, which caused the air turnback. The open panel is the stated condition, so the label is OPEN.

OPEN

Label: MISINSTALLED. The emergency exit arrow lens was pointing the wrong way, and the fix was a correctly oriented lens. That indicates it was installed backwards.

MISINSTALLED

Door hard to open and close, which fits STIFF or BINDS. The fix was replacing the threshold and trim piece, which points to the door binding on them, so BINDS fits best.

BINDS

Testing found that the tank units F4L and F6L had capacitance outside limits, so the condition of the failed part is out of limits.

OUT OF LIMITS

Lock was difficult to operate and fixed by lubrication, so the condition is stiffness (or lack of lubrication). "STIFF" fits a difficult-to-operate lock best.

STIFF

Rev disagree message was intermittent. The fix was rigging the stow switches, so the switches were out of rig. The failed condition could be labeled "OUT OF RIG", but the report itself describes the symptom as "intermittent", and the corrective action shows the switches were misrigged.

INTERMITTENT

Choosing a label means weighing the indication against the part's actual condition. The trigger was an L FIRE FAIL amber CAS message, which on its own suggests WARNING MESSAGE or FAULT MESSAGE. The part condition is less clear: inspections and swaps found no defects, yet the heating element in zone A was eventually replaced.

Because the fault appeared only in turbulence and never showed during testing, it was behaving intermittently. Still, the event is defined by the CAS message, and the condition is best captured as the fault indication that appeared. A "FIRE FAIL" message is a fault annunciation rather than a fire warning, so FAULT MESSAGE fits better than WARNING MESSAGE.

FAULT MESSAGE

The report opens with "tire 7 deflated" and says it was replaced because it "blown out", with burst or flat-spotted tire inspections performed. The deflation is the condition stated in the report title, so that best describes the failed part. "Burst" and "blew out" also fit, but they describe the cause rather than the reported condition.

DEFLATED

The part at fault is the O-ring sealing the hydraulic filter bowl to the filter base. The report says it "failed", which let hydraulic fluid leak out of the reservoir, so the condition of that O-ring is best described as leaking.

LEAKING

Contour of chord does not match — likely mismanufactured part, or deformed/distorted. "Contour can not match" during modification suggests the part is mismanufactured or doesn't fit; the most likely label is MISMANUFACTURED.

MISMANUFACTURED

The light fails to come on, so the condition is that the part does not work. "INOPERATIVE" fits that best.

INOPERATIVE

Squib (cartridge) was removed because its time limit was reached, which points to EXPIRED rather than OUT OF DATE.

EXPIRED

Slide unravelled during maintenance — that's an unpacked slide. The label is UNPACKED.

UNPACKED

The report has two findings: the bleed detection loop was contacting the bleed duct, and the RH HASOV insulation muff was improperly installed. The warning itself is a symptom rather than the condition of a part. The first finding, a loop touching the duct and needing relocation, fits INTERFERENCE better than WARNING LIGHT or WARNING MESSAGE. The second finding would fit MISINSTALLED, but the loop contact appears to be the primary cause of the warning, so INTERFERENCE is the stronger choice.

INTERFERENCE

Duct with a hole — the closest match among the labels is PERFORATED.

PERFORATED

Charred debris was found inside the captain's pitot probe. That foreign material restricted the probe and caused the captain's airspeed to read low. Possible labels include OBSTRUCTED, CONTAMINATED, FOD, BLOCKED and CLOGGED. Debris sitting in the probe fits CONTAMINATED or OBSTRUCTED best, and OBSTRUCTED is the more common label for pitot blockage.

OBSTRUCTED

Engine surges were reported, and the borescope found HPC stage 4 blades damaged beyond limits. The candidates are SURGES or DAMAGED. The defective part identified is the blades, whose condition is damaged, so the condition of that part is the better fit than the symptom.

DAMAGED

Mis-drilled holes on a repaired part point to a prior repair done incorrectly, which fits MISREPAIRED better than MISMANUFACTURED.

MISREPAIRED

Door difficult to open, fixed by lubrication. "LACK OF LUBE" fits the cause, while "STIFF" or "BINDS" describe the symptom. Since the corrective action was lube, I'll go with LACK OF LUBE.

LACK OF LUBE

The part that failed is the engine, and the report says the left engine stalled after takeoff. The LPT blade damage is what the corrective action found, but the reported failure condition is the stall.

STALLED

Oxygen bottle reading 0, suspected leak. Possible labels: LEAKING, DEPLETED, EMPTY, LOW PRESSURE. The leak was only "possible" and the gauge read 0, so the bottle was depleted. EMPTY and DEPLETED both fit, and DEPLETED is common for oxygen.

DEPLETED

Debris was blocking the view window, so the indicator itself was fine and its view was obstructed. The candidates are "OBSTRUCTED", "BLOCKED" and "FOD". "OBSTRUCTED" fits best, since the report says the flag was "obscured".

OBSTRUCTED

The report shows the APU exhaust temperature (CT5ATP) at or above the 605-degree threshold, which is an over-temperature condition.

OVERTEMP
